name: Crimean Tatar
family: Turkic, Kipchak (West Kipchak, with strong Oghuz influence)
variety: Standard Crimean Tatar, based on the Central (Orta yolaq) dialect; Latin script (Cyrillic also in use)
sources: Kavitskaya, Darya (2010). Crimean Tatar. Lincom Europa.

McCollum, Adam G. & Kavitskaya, Darya (2018). Non-iterative vowel harmony in Crimean Tatar. Proceedings of the 35th West Coast Conference on Formal Linguistics, 259-268. Cascadilla Proceedings Project.
Berta, Árpád (1998). West Kipchak languages. In Lars Johanson & Éva Á. Csató (eds.), The Turkic Languages. Routledge.
contrasts: eight vowels: high versus non-high, front versus back, rounded versus unrounded
voiced versus voiceless stops and affricates
velar /k ɡ/ versus uvular /q/ and the fricatives /x ɣ/ (spelt h, ğ)
high vowels are short and lax, non-high vowels are longer
allophony: the high vowels are short and reduced; /i/ and /ɯ/ are both realised close to a centralised [ɪ] although they remain distinct phonemes (Kavitskaya 2010)
/k ɡ/ are fronted next to front vowels; /q/ and /ɣ/ occur with back vowels in native words
the letter h stands for the velar fricative [x]; a glottal [h] belongs to the southern dialect
/l/ is velarised next to back vowels
stem-final /p q k/ are voiced before vowel-initial suffixes (kitap, kitabı)
the southern dialect has [x] for standard /q/; the northern dialect has [q] for /x/ and [p] for /f/
phonotactics: no onset clusters in native words
coda clusters are sonorant or fricative + obstruent (dört, qırq, halq)
backness harmony in native words and suffixes

rounding harmony is not iterative in the standard (central) dialect: it rounds a high vowel of the second syllable only (tuzluq, tuzluğı); the southern dialect rounds all following high vowels, the northern dialect none
/ŋ/ does not begin a word; /f v ʒ/ are frequent in loans

stress.type: fixed final by default, with morphological exceptions
stress.rule: Stress falls on the last syllable of the word; unstressable suffixes and particles (negative -ma/-me, question -mı/-mi, predicative personal endings) leave it on the syllable before them.
stress.cues: not instrumentally studied in the sources used

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: the high vowels are short, centralised and may be dropped in unstressed syllables; non-high vowels keep their quality

length.notes: No vowel length contrast. Geminates occur in a few stems (elli 'fifty'), in loans and at morpheme boundaries.

intonation.declarative: rise on the final stressed syllable of non-final phrases, fall at the end of the statement
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the particle -mı/-mi/-mu/-mü; pitch is high on the syllable before the particle
intonation.wh_question: prominence on the question word, final fall
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: rise to a high on the final stressed syllable
intonation.notes: Low confidence: no instrumental study of Crimean Tatar intonation was available to me; the entries follow the general pattern of the better described Turkic languages (Turkish, Kazakh).

problems: a palatal glide is put before every e and most i, which palatalises the preceding consonant in the Russian way (men gives [mʲen], ev gives [ʲef], kelmedi gives [cʲelmʲedɪ]); the descriptions of Crimean Tatar have no such palatalisation
word-final z, v and j are devoiced to [s f ʃ] by rule (qız gives [qɯs]); the standard language keeps final /z/ voiced
i after most consonants is a mid central vowel (F1 500, F2 1412 Hz) and ı is F1 448, F2 1280 Hz: both are mid rather than high, and the difference between them is small
ö is a mid central vowel with the same formant targets as schwa (525 and 1441 Hz)
unstressable suffixes are covered only in part: the negative -ma/-me and the question particle are stressed (kelmedi gets final stress)
good: final stress is written into the vowel rules
q, ñ [ŋ], ğ [ɣ] and h [x] are present; k and g are palatal before front vowels; l is velarised next to back vowels
vowel harmony follows from the spelling; a list of about 500 words covers names and exceptions

notes: The voice is marked 'status testing' in eSpeak NG. Its p t k are unaspirated; the sources used here do not document the degree of aspiration in Crimean Tatar.
